rv.q: “Two Sisters and a Piano,” now receiving a semi-fulfilling production at Writers Theatre in suburban Glencoe, first premiered in the late 1990s, and its thematic and lyrical richness helped build Cruz’s formidable reputation.
Light on plot but lush in atmosphere, this sometimes mesmerizing, sometimes frustrating play examines how these two artistic souls — Maria Celia is a writer, Sofia a pianist — endure their captivity.
Once the ball gets rolling, “Two Sisters and a Piano” is an irresistible force.
Writers Theatre presents a thought-provoking production that’s made even richer by its exquisite staging and fine performances.
San Miguel and Mendoza Castro draw the audience completely into their performances, and it is difficult to leave these compelling characters behind.
What it works best as is a character study, giving us two fascinating, complex characters that make us want to lean in and learn more about them.
Cruz's story gives a human dimension to the costs of enforcing ideology over empathy.
In Writers’ revival, ably staged by Lisa Portes, dancing becomes an expression of unbridled joy for these young women.
But the most interesting parts are the relief provided by the scenes with Victor the piano tuner and Sofia, who finally cracks under the oppressive weight of her seclusion.
I thought that every detail of this production was solid.

cn.t: Cruz's poetic drama about Cuban sisters under house arrest earns mixed-to-positive reviews, with critics praising strong performances and lyrical writing while noting the production feels only semi-fulfilling.
